messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: function template defaults
parts:
Daniel and I came up with a way to merge the
policied and unpolicied function calls using
template defaults. Daniel then went and pushed
this through the library. It all worked fine
on our Macs. Then he tried other compilers and
platforms, which couldn't handle the function
template defaults.

The current standard allows defaults for class
template parameters, but not for function template
parameters.

Eventually, the compilers should catch up to the
new C++11 standard, but I think it'd be nice to run
with the current crop until then.

So I'm suggesting that we switch our functions back
to Boost style for now at least, such as

template <typename T1, typename T2>
inline typename calc<T2,T3>::type
foo(const T1& x1, const T2& x2) {
return foo(x1,x2,policy<>::type);
}

template <typename T1, typename T2, typename P>
inline typename calc<T1,T2>::type
foo(const T1& x1, const T2& x2, const P& /* ignore */) {
... use P() if necessary ...
}

The inline combined with the resolution of the
default policy at compile time and the second function
not paying attention to the actual param means there's
at least no run-time overhead.

The downside is that there's now double the doc
to write, though I think the resulting unpolicied function,
which is what you almost always want to use, will be
clearer to most users.

- Bob

wrote:

Daniel and I came up with a way to merge the
policied and unpolicied function calls using
template defaults.  Daniel then went and pushed
this through the library.  It all worked fine
on our Macs.  Then he tried other compilers and
platforms, which couldn't handle the function
template defaults.

The current standard allows defaults for class
template parameters, but not for function template
parameters.

Eventually, the compilers should catch up to the
new C++11 standard, but I think it'd be nice to run
with the current crop until then.

So I'm suggesting that we switch our functions back
to Boost style for now at least, such as

template<typename T1, typename T2>
inline typename calc<T2,T3>::type
foo(const T1&  x1, const T2&  x2) {
   return foo(x1,x2,policy<>::type);
}

template<typename T1, typename T2, typename P>
inline typename calc<T1,T2>::type
foo(const T1&  x1, const T2&  x2, const P&  /* ignore */) {
   ... use P() if necessary ...
}

The inline combined with the resolution of the
default policy at compile time and the second function
not paying attention to the actual param means there's
at least no run-time overhead.

The downside is that there's now double the doc
to write, though I think the resulting unpolicied function,
which is what you almost always want to use, will be
clearer to most users.

- Bob

>>>>>>>>>>> to Boost style for now at least, such as
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> template<typename T1, typename T2>
>>>>>>>>>>> inline typename calc<T2,T3>::type
>>>>>>>>>>> foo(const T1&  x1, const T2&  x2) {
>>>>>>>>>>>    return foo(x1,x2,policy<>::type);
>>>>>>>>>>> }
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> template<typename T1, typename T2, typename P>
>>>>>>>>>>> inline typename calc<T1,T2>::type
>>>>>>>>>>> foo(const T1&  x1, const T2&  x2, const P&  /* ignore */) {
>>>>>>>>>>>    ... use P() if necessary ...
>>>>>>>>>>> }
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> The inline combined with the resolution of the
>>>>>>>>>>> default policy at compile time and the second function
>>>>>>>>>>> not paying attention to the actual param means there's
>>>>>>>>>>> at least no run-time overhead.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> The downside is that there's now double the doc
>>>>>>>>>>> to write, though I think the resulting unpolicied function,
>>>>>>>>>>> which is what you almost always want to use, will be
>>>>>>>>>>> clearer to most users.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> - Bob
